extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, aesthetics, and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic/aesthetic criteria and principles for judging poetry and fine art from an Aristotelian and classical-critical perspective, including aims (ends), methods of composition, audience standards, and moral/functionalist claims about art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal (καθόλου)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is essentially ideal and conveys the general or universal truth (το καθόλου) through particular, concrete representations; its apparent individualities must be representative of a class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle, Coleridge and Goethe agree that while poetry deals with particulars, the poetic imagination abstracts and thereby lets the universal shine through the individual. The 'universal' is not a single abstract truth but the set of truths that meet in the individual. Coleridge warns that this is not mere allegory (not 'a general idea embodied in a particular'), but the artistic generalisation of a particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic generalisation: particular → universal by treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet generalises the particular case by artistic treatment: from individual states he abstracts universal kinds, then reclothes them in diverse names and fates so they 'steal access' to the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted lines (Sir John Davies via Coleridge) illustrate that the process is not to embody an abstract idea in a single example (allegory) but to transform and particularise so that the particular becomes universal through treatment. Goethe and Coleridge stress that poets work from sensuous impressions and elaboration rather than by trying to embody abstractions directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition method: outline general plot then fill details
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice (attributed to Aristotle) that a poet should set forth the plot in its general idea (a bare sketch, καθόλου), abstracting accidental features of time, place, and persons, and afterwards fill it in with detail, incident and proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes this is a recommended order of composition whether drawing on tradition or invention, but also questions its practical value and calls attention to the distinct senses of καθόλου (broad outline vs universal truth). The method can be considered 'faulty and unpoetical' in practice even though it is logically separable from the doctrine of the universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters clothed with generic attributes yet particularised
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in poetry should be clothed with generic/class attributes so they represent a class, but these class characteristics must be so modified and particularised that they do not destroy individual distinctiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge advises that class characteristics constitute the instructiveness of a character, but are to be particularised in each person (e.g., Shakespearean characters) so life itself does not excite more sense of individuality than the dramatic person does. The balance of generic and particular is essential: involution of the universal in the individual, with the individual form uppermost.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of fine art: pleasure / rational enjoyment (πρὸς ἡδονήν / πρὸς διαγωγήν)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end (telos) of fine art is to give pleasure or a rational enjoyment of leisure rather than to provide mere utility; art's distinctive aim is aesthetic pleasure or elevated delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes fine from useful arts: fine arts minister to pleasure (including higher forms associated with leisure and speculative thought). The pleasure is not incidental but the proper end, though it admits of higher or lower kinds, and is to be understood relative to the kind of audience and the art-form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish higher and lower pleasures; aim for higher/aesthetic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures produced by art vary in quality: harmless pastime pleasures (παιδιά) differ from the higher, noble pleasure (διαγωγή) connected with leisure and intellectual or aesthetic contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: music may be a toy or an element of highest happiness depending on the audience. Aristotle implies that serious arts (e.g., tragedy) aim at the higher form of pleasure; comedy and lower art forms typically produce pastime-type pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: The spectator's/audience's pleasure is the art's end (not the maker's)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's theory regards the end of art as the pleasurable impression produced upon the mind of the spectator or listener, not the inward satisfaction of the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist may share in the pleasure only insofar as he participates as a member of the public. Thus evaluation focuses on the effect upon viewers/listeners rather than the creator's private satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of judgment: the cultivated public / man of sound aesthetic instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Final appeal in aesthetic judgment is to a cultivated public or a person of trained/sound aesthetic instincts (ὁ χαρίεις), analogous to the man of practical wisdom (ὁ φρόνιμος) in ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle prefers popular judgment but of a cultivated class; different audiences (free/educated vs vulgar) enjoy different kinds of music/arts. The 'ideal spectator' who represents a normally constituted humanity is the rule and standard for taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic effect must be appropriate, distinctive and non-arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure produced must be the distinctive pleasure proper to that art, not any chance or arbitrary pleasure; the art's success is measured by how well it produces its characteristic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, tragedy's characteristic pleasure is distinct from comedic pleasure. Works that gratify audience weakness (e.g., forced happy endings) may give pleasure but not the art's characteristic pleasure and so fail artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must arouse pity and fear (its distinctive function)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic action has an inherent capacity to call forth pity and fear; the degree to which it achieves this is the test of artistic merit in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's rules for tragedy (plot design, character selection, recognition, etc.) flow from this primary requirement. The pleasure from tragedy arises from the union of the pitiable and the terrible and must be prepared by the poet in the material and construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper construction of plot (unity and structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot construction must be appropriate to the art's function—structured so as to produce the required emotional effect (e.g., pity/fear in tragedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text refers to Aristotle's prescriptions on plot (unity, proper arrangement of incidents) as deriving from the need to arouse the art's characteristic emotional responses; an ill-constructed plot will fail in its end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and shaping of character (ideal hero aligned to function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters—especially the tragic hero—must be shaped to serve the dramatic function, possessing qualities that make the elicitation of pity and fear appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal hero's character is guided by the primary requirement of the genre; generic attributes may be used but must be particularised so the character performs his role in the plot's moral/emotional economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of recognition (anagnorisis) and peripeteia
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of recognition and reversals must be employed in the best form to serve the plot's emotional and intellectual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's rules include determinations about how recognition and change of fortune best operate to achieve the tragic pleasure; the 'best form of recognition' is part of the structural tools to realize the genre's end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter: art should engage human and mental life, not mere likenesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art (especially poetry) is concerned with human and mental life; pictorial or plastic imitations of lower forms of animal life fall outside the proper range of artistic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower imitative works may display workmanship and produce a pleasure analogous to admiration of nature's adaptation of means to ends, but they do not belong to the artistic domain concerned with human/mental phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's moral/educational function (traditional view)
rubrics_metrics.description: A traditional criterion holds that poetry has a direct moral purpose and functions as a teacher (ψυχαγωγία/παιδεία)—Homer as instructive exemplar; poetry introduces youth to life and character and gives pleasurable instruction in ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts this with Aristotle's view of poetry as primarily an emotional delight. Plutarch and others insist poetry is preparatory to philosophy, opening young minds to ethical doctrines; Aristophanes likewise claims moral teaching as a purpose of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's moral character relates to poetic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of a poet was traditionally thought inseparable from the excellence of the human being: 'No one can be a good poet who is not first a good man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage reflects a long-standing Greek sentiment (Strabo, Plutarch) that ethical worth and civic virtue inform poetic authority and instructive power; moral fitness of the poet affects the value of his teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid striving to embody abstractions; work from vivid impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should not attempt to embody abstract ideas directly; rather they receive sensuous, animated impressions and artistically round them off to reproduce those impressions so others may receive similar impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goethe's account of his creative process is cited: he received impressions of a sensuous, varied kind and only artistically elaborated them; Coleridge similarly warns against recommending abstractions as the method of poetry.
